value.overview: The White-winged Dove (Zenaida asiatica) is a medium-sized, warm gray-brown dove named for the broad white wing patch visible in flight. It is native to the southern United States, Mexico, Central America, and parts of the Caribbean. The species commonly uses open, warm landscapes rather than dense forest and can adapt to farms, towns, gardens, and dry woodland. In Costa Rica, it is especially associated with the dry Pacific lowlands and is locally common to abundant there.
value.classification: The White-winged Dove belongs to the dove and pigeon family Columbidae and the order Columbiformes. Its scientific name is Zenaida asiatica.
value.identification: This dove has a bulky body, rounded head, short tail, and mostly grayish-brown plumage. The most distinctive feature is the conspicuous white patch along the wing, especially obvious during flight, together with broad white tips on the outer tail feathers. Adults usually show orange to reddish eyes, a bluish bare eye-ring, a black bill, and pinkish-red legs. A dark cheek mark and subtle purplish or bronze iridescence on the neck may be visible, particularly in males. It is heavier and shorter-tailed than a Mourning Dove.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from the southwestern and southern United States through Mexico and Central America, with additional populations in the Caribbean. In Costa Rica, it is a permanent resident mainly in the northwestern Pacific dry zone, extending south approximately to Jacó and usually occurring below about 500 meters, though it is occasionally found higher. It also sometimes reaches the Central Valley and San José. Typical habitats include savannas, dry woodland edges, thorn scrub, cactus areas, agricultural land, villages, and suburbs, especially where scattered trees and nearby feeding areas occur.
value.migrationStatus: White-winged Doves are resident in southern parts of their range, including much of Costa Rica, while northern populations make seasonal movements. Costa Rica supports both resident birds and wintering migrants from North America, with larger numbers reported in Guanacaste roughly from November through May. Movements within Costa Rica may also be local or elevation-related.
value.breeding: White-winged Doves usually build a simple, shallow platform of coarse sticks. In Costa Rica, nests may be placed about 2 to 8 meters above the ground in thorn trees, shrubs, cacti, mangroves, or other suitable vegetation. The usual clutch is one or two white eggs. In the Costa Rican dry Pacific region, breeding has been reported mainly from January through March, although timing can vary with local rainfall, food availability, and habitat conditions. Both parents participate in incubation and care of the young.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of seeds and other plant material, including grains, fruits, berries, and seeds from grasses and dry-zone plants. White-winged Doves commonly forage on the ground in open areas, agricultural fields, gardens, and around settlements. They may also visit elevated feeders. Feeding sites are often close to trees or other cover used for perching and roosting, and the birds may gather in groups where food is plentiful.
value.behavior: This is a social dove that often travels and roosts in flocks, sometimes numbering many individuals. It spends much of the day perched in trees or searching the ground for food, and it commonly visits water sources in warm, dry landscapes. Its flight is direct and fast, with the white wing patches becoming highly conspicuous. The species has a distinctive repetitive cooing song and may become accustomed to human-modified environments, including towns and suburban neighborhoods.

conservation.populationTrend: Broad-scale North American monitoring has indicated an increasing population in recent decades, although trends may differ among regions and subspecies. A reliable long-term population trend specifically for Costa Rica is not established.
